Section 3.3 of Lock⁵ turns the bootstrap idea into a working method for
**confidence intervals**: take a bootstrap sample by resampling the original
data *with replacement* (matching the original sample size and the structure
of the statistic), compute the statistic for each bootstrap sample, and use
the spread of the resulting **bootstrap distribution** to measure how much the
statistic varies from sample to sample. The bootstrap distribution is
centered at the value of the original sample statistic, and its standard
deviation estimates the **standard error (SE)**. Section 3.3 builds a 95%
interval as **statistic ± 2·SE**; in Section 3.4 the same interval is read
directly from the percentiles of the bootstrap distribution, and we show both
below — when the bootstrap distribution is reasonably symmetric and
bell-shaped the two agree closely, while for skewed or lumpy distributions
they can differ, a useful visual warning. A confidence interval also doubles
as a two-sided test: a value *inside* the interval is plausible for the
parameter, a value *outside* it is not.
The exercises below are from *Statistics: Unlocking the Power of Data*
(Lock⁵, 3rd ed., pp. 256–262). Skill Builders 3.80–3.85 recognize possible
bootstrap samples and read centers, standard errors, and intervals off
bootstrap distributions; 3.86–3.103 build intervals for proportions and
differences in proportions; 3.100–3.111 apply the method to means, a
correlation, and a standard deviation, using real Lock⁵ datasets loaded
below. All executable bootstraps use 5000 replicates with seed 2026, so the
intervals are reproducible; the book's printed intervals (from StatKey runs)
agree to within Monte Carlo wobble.

```{python}
#| include: false
import os
from pathlib import Path
_root = Path.cwd()
while not (_root / "_quarto.yml").exists():
    _root = _root.parent
os.chdir(_root)
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt, seaborn as sns
sns.set_theme(style="whitegrid")

def boot_stats(groups, stat_fn, reps=5000, seed=2026):
    """Bootstrap statistics: resample each group in `groups` with replacement,
    apply `stat_fn` to the list of resampled arrays, repeat `reps` times."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    out = np.empty(reps)
    for i in range(reps):
        res = [g[rng.integers(0, len(g), len(g))] for g in groups]
        out[i] = stat_fn(res)
    return out

def boot_plot(boots, xlabel, bins=30, figsize=(6, 3)):
    """Histogram of a bootstrap distribution with the middle 95% percentile lines."""
    lo, hi = np.percentile(boots, [2.5, 97.5])
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=figsize)
    sns.histplot(x=boots, bins=bins, ax=ax, color="#4c72b0")
    for v in (lo, hi):
        ax.axvline(v, color="#c44e52", ls="--", lw=1)
    ax.set_xlabel(xlabel)
    ax.set_ylabel("Bootstrap statistics")
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

def boot_row(label, stat, boots, digits=3):
    """One-row summary: statistic, bootstrap SE, statistic ± 2·SE, percentile CI."""
    se = boots.std(ddof=1)
    lo, hi = np.percentile(boots, [2.5, 97.5])
    return pd.Series({
        label: round(float(stat), digits),
        "Bootstrap SE": round(float(se), digits),
        "Statistic ± 2·SE": f"({stat - 2 * se:.{digits}f}, {stat + 2 * se:.{digits}f})",
        "95% percentile CI": f"({lo:.{digits}f}, {hi:.{digits}f})",
    })

def yes_no(n_yes, n_no):
    """Binary array: 1 = yes/agree, 0 = no."""
    return np.repeat([1.0, 0.0], [n_yes, n_no])
```

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Exercise 3.80

*(Skill Builder 1: possible bootstrap samples?)* Original sample: 17, 10, 15,
21, 13, 18 ($n = 6$). A bootstrap sample must have exactly 6 values, each
drawn *with replacement* from the original six — so every value must be one of
10, 13, 15, 17, 18, 21, and repeats are allowed.

- **(a) 10, 12, 17, 18, 20, 21 — No.** The values 12 and 20 are not in the
  original sample.
- **(b) 10, 15, 17 — No.** Only 3 values; a bootstrap sample must match the
  original sample size of 6.
- **(c) 10, 13, 15, 17, 18, 21 — Yes.** The original six values, each drawn
  once (each is in the original sample, and drawing each exactly once is
  allowed).
- **(d) 18, 13, 21, 17, 15, 13, 10 — No.** Seven values — the wrong size.
- **(e) 13, 10, 21, 10, 18, 17 — Yes.** Every value comes from the original
  sample, the size is 6, and the repeated 10 is fine when resampling with
  replacement.

## Exercise 3.81

*(Skill Builder 1)* Original sample: 85, 72, 79, 97, 88 ($n = 5$). Each
bootstrap sample must have 5 values drawn with replacement from the original
five.

- **(a) 79, 79, 97, 85, 88 — Yes.** All values are in the original sample; the
  repeated 79 is allowed.
- **(b) 72, 79, 85, 88, 97 — Yes.** The original values in a different order.
- **(c) 85, 88, 97, 72 — No.** Only 4 values — the wrong size.
- **(d) 88, 97, 81, 78, 85 — No.** The values 81 and 78 are not in the
  original sample.
- **(e) 97, 85, 79, 85, 97 — Yes.** All values from the original sample,
  repeats allowed, correct size.
- **(f) 72, 72, 79, 72, 79 — Yes.** Same — only 72s and 79s, but only those
  two values are needed and repeats are allowed.

## Exercise 3.82

*(Skill Builder 2: estimate the statistic, standard error, and 95% confidence
interval from Figure 3.19(a), a bootstrap distribution for a sample
proportion. Values read from the graph; answers may vary slightly.)*

- **Statistic: $\hat p \approx 0.7$** — a bootstrap distribution is centered at
  the original sample proportion, and the dotplot peaks at about 0.7.
- **Standard error: $SE \approx 0.05$** — the bootstrap proportions spread
  over roughly 0.5 to 0.9, a range of about 0.4, which is about 4 standard
  errors on either side of the center... equivalently, most values lie within
  about 0.1 of 0.7.
- **95% confidence interval: $0.7 \pm 2(0.05)$, from about 0.6 to 0.8.**
- **Parameter: $p$**, the population proportion that the sample proportion
  estimates.

## Exercise 3.83

*(Skill Builder 2: Figure 3.19(b), a bootstrap distribution for a sample
mean.)*

- **Statistic: $\bar x \approx 25$** — the bootstrap means center at about 25.
- **Standard error: $SE \approx 3$** — the bootstrap means spread over roughly
  16 to 34 (range 18 ≈ 6 SEs).
- **95% confidence interval: $25 \pm 2(3) = 19$ to $31$.**
- **Parameter: $\mu$**, the population mean.

## Exercise 3.86

*(Skill Builder 3: single proportion — in a random sample of 100 people, 35
agree.)* The sample proportion is $\hat p = 35/100 = 0.35$. We bootstrap by
resampling 100 values with replacement from the sample of 35 agreements and
65 disagreements and computing the proportion in each bootstrap sample:

- **Bootstrap SE ≈ 0.048.**
- **95% confidence interval: $0.35 \pm 2(0.048)$, from about 0.25 to 0.45.**
- Interpretation: we are 95% sure that the proportion of the population that
  agrees is between about 0.25 and 0.45.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Bootstrap distribution of the sample proportion, 35 agree in a sample of 100
sample = yes_no(35, 65)
boots = boot_stats([sample], lambda r: r[0].mean())
boot_plot(boots, "Bootstrap sample proportions")
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
boot_row("Sample proportion", 0.35, boots).to_string()
```

## Exercise 3.90

**Hitchhiker Snails.** Biologist Shinichiro Wada fed 174 live snails to
birds; 26 of the snails were excreted live out the other end.

- **(a)** The best estimate for the proportion of all such snails to live
  after being eaten by a bird is the sample proportion
  $\hat p = 26/174 \approx 0.15$.
- **(b)** The bootstrap distribution in Figure 3.20 (mean 0.15, st. dev.
  0.028) gives **SE ≈ 0.028**.
- **(c)** $0.15 \pm 2(0.028) = 0.094$ to $0.206$: we are 95% sure that the
  proportion of all snails of this type that would survive being eaten by a
  bird is between about 0.09 and 0.21. Our own 5000-replicate bootstrap
  below gives an almost identical interval.
- **(d) Yes.** Since 0.20 lies within the interval from part (c), it is
  plausible that 20% of all snails of this type live after being eaten by a
  bird.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Bootstrap distribution of the proportion of snails that survive being eaten by a bird
snails = yes_no(26, 174 - 26)
boots = boot_stats([snails], lambda r: r[0].mean())
boot_plot(boots, "Bootstrap sample proportions")
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
boot_row("Proportion surviving", 26 / 174, boots).to_string()
```

## Exercise 3.91

**Are You Distracted by Off-Task Technology in Class?** The bootstrap
distribution of the sample proportion of students often distracted by
off-task technology use is shown in Figure 3.21.

- **(a)** The best estimate of the proportion of all students who would
  answer yes is the center of the bootstrap distribution, **about 0.49**.
- **(b)** **SE ≈ 0.025.** The bootstrap proportions spread over roughly 0.40
  to 0.58, so most fall within about 0.05 of the center and half of that
  range, about 0.025, is a typical distance from 0.49.
- **(c)** $0.49 \pm 2(0.025) = 0.44$ to $0.54$: we are 95% sure that the
  proportion of all students who feel they are often distracted during class
  by off-task use of technology is between 0.44 and 0.54.

## Exercise 3.92

**Can You Tell a Story about Your Parents?** Of 260 US young adults (around
age 18) who were asked, 244 could recall a story a parent had told them
about when the parent was young.

- **(a)** $\hat p = 244/260 \approx 0.938$. Bootstrapping the 260 responses
  gives **SE ≈ 0.015** and a 95% confidence interval of
  $0.938 \pm 2(0.015) = 0.908$ to $0.968$: we are 95% sure that the
  proportion of all US young adults who can recall such a family story is
  between about 0.91 and 0.97.
- **(b) Yes.** The entire confidence interval lies above 0.90, so a
  proportion of 0.90 or less is not plausible for the population — the
  claim that *more than* 90% can retell a family story is supported.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Bootstrap distribution of the proportion of young adults who can recall a family story
story = yes_no(244, 260 - 244)
boots = boot_stats([story], lambda r: r[0].mean())
boot_plot(boots, "Bootstrap sample proportions")
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
boot_row("Proportion recalling", 244 / 260, boots).to_string()
```

## Exercise 3.94

**Do Teen Problems Differ Based on Income Level?** From Table 3.10, teens
saying anxiety/depression is a major problem: below \$75,000 — 386 of 536;
above \$75,000 — 258 of 384.

- **(a)** Below \$75,000: $\hat p_L = 386/536 \approx 0.720$. Above \$75,000:
  $\hat p_H = 258/384 \approx 0.672$.
- **(b)** The sample statistic is $\hat p_L - \hat p_H = 0.720 - 0.672 =
  0.048$, estimating the parameter $p_L - p_H$.
- **(c)** Bootstrapping each group separately (536 and 384 values, with
  replacement) gives **SE ≈ 0.031**.
- **(d)** $0.048 \pm 2(0.031) = -0.013$ to $0.110$.
- **(e) No.** Since 0 is within the interval, a difference of zero between
  the two income groups is plausible — the data do not convince us that the
  proportions differ.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Bootstrap distribution of the difference in proportions, lower income minus higher income teens
low = yes_no(386, 536 - 386)
high = yes_no(258, 384 - 258)
boots = boot_stats([low, high], lambda r: r[0].mean() - r[1].mean())
boot_plot(boots, "Bootstrap difference in proportions (low - high)")
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
boot_row("Difference (low - high)", 386 / 536 - 258 / 384, boots).to_string()
```

## Exercise 3.95

**Ants on a Sandwich.** A student in Australia counted the ants that climbed
on a piece of peanut butter sandwich left on the ground, eight times
(Table 3.11): 43, 59, 22, 25, 36, 47, 19, 21.

- **(a)** Computed below: **$\bar x = 34.0$ ants, $s = 14.63$.**
- **(b)** Write each of the eight values on a slip of paper, put the slips in
  a bag, and mix well. Draw one slip, record the value, *return it*, and
  repeat until 8 values are recorded — that is one bootstrap sample.
  Average the 8 values to get one bootstrap statistic (a bootstrap sample
  mean).
- **(c)** The bootstrap distribution should be roughly **bell-shaped** (the
  original sample is roughly symmetric) and **centered at 34**, the original
  sample mean.
- **(d)** The parameter is $\mu$, the **mean number of ants** that would
  climb on a piece of peanut butter sandwich left near this ant hill; the
  best estimate is $\bar x = 34$.
- **(e)** With SE = 4.85: $34 \pm 2(4.85) = 24.3$ to $43.7$. We are 95% sure
  that the mean number of ants on such a sandwich piece is between about 24
  and 44. (Our 5000-replicate bootstrap below gives SE ≈ 4.9 and an almost
  identical interval.)

```{python}
#| echo: false
ants = np.array([43, 59, 22, 25, 36, 47, 19, 21], dtype=float)
pd.Series({"Mean": round(ants.mean(), 1),
           "StDev": round(ants.std(ddof=1), 2)}).to_string()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Bootstrap distribution of the mean number of ants on a peanut butter sandwich
boots = boot_stats([ants], lambda r: r[0].mean())
boot_plot(boots, "Bootstrap sample means")
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
boot_row("Sample mean", ants.mean(), boots, digits=1).to_string()
```

## Exercise 3.96

**Brain Hippocampal Size.** We use the $n = 25$ participants in the control
group of the football/hippocampus study (Exercise 2.165,
`FootballBrain` data) to estimate average brain hippocampus volume for all
non-football-playing people.

- **(a) Dotplot I (values from about 6000 to 10000) shows the original
  data; Dotplot II (values from about 7000 to 8200) shows the bootstrap
  distribution.** Bootstrap statistics vary less than individual data values,
  so the bootstrap dotplot is the tighter one.
- **(b)** Both plots are centered near **7600**, so $\bar x \approx 7600\ \mu L$
  (computed from the data: $\bar x = 7602.6$).
- **(c)** The bootstrap means in Dotplot II spread over roughly 7000 to 8200,
  so **SE ≈ 200 μL** (our bootstrap gives SE ≈ 206).
- **(d) Larger.** The standard deviation of the original data ($s \approx
  1074\ \mu L$) is much larger than the standard error — dividing by
  $\sqrt{n} = \sqrt{25} = 5$ shrinks the spread of means far below the spread
  of individuals.
- **(e)** $7600 \pm 2(200) = 7200$ to $8000\ \mu L$: we are 95% sure that the
  mean hippocampal volume for all non-football-playing people is between
  about 7200 and 8000 μL.

*Data:* `data/ch02/FootballBrain.csv`, from
<https://www.lock5stat.com/datasets3e/FootballBrain.csv>:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Bootstrap distribution of the mean hippocampal volume for the control group
hipp = pd.read_csv("data/ch02/FootballBrain.csv")
ctrl = hipp.loc[hipp.Group == "Control", "Hipp"].dropna().to_numpy(float)
boots = boot_stats([ctrl], lambda r: r[0].mean())
boot_plot(boots, "Bootstrap sample means (μL)")
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
boot_row("Sample mean (μL)", ctrl.mean(), boots, digits=0).to_string()
```

## Exercise 3.97

**Rats with Compassion.** In the study, 23 of the 30 rats freed a trapped
rat, even with chocolate as a distraction. We estimate the proportion of all
rats that would show empathy in this way.

- **(a)** The parameter is $p$, the proportion of all rats that would free a
  trapped rat; the best estimate is $\hat p = 23/30 \approx 0.767$.
- **(b)** Write **yes** on 23 slips of paper and **no** on 7 slips, mix them,
  draw one slip, record it, *return it*, and repeat 30 times. The proportion
  of yes values among the 30 draws is one bootstrap statistic.
- **(c)** The bootstrap distribution below (from the `CompassionateRats`
  data) is roughly bell-shaped and centered at 0.767, with **SE ≈ 0.077**.
- **(d)** $0.767 \pm 2(0.077) = 0.613$ to $0.921$: we are 95% sure that the
  proportion of rats likely to show empathy is between about 0.61 and 0.92.
  (The percentile interval from our run sits slightly lower — the bootstrap
  distribution is a bit skewed left.)

*Data:* `data/ch03/CompassionateRats.csv`, from
<https://www.lock5stat.com/datasets3e/CompassionateRats.csv>:

```{python}
#| echo: false

rats = pd.read_csv("data/ch03/CompassionateRats.csv")
empathy = (rats["Empathy"] == "yes").to_numpy(float)
boots = boot_stats([empathy], lambda r: r[0].mean())
```

## Exercise 3.98

**Are Female Rats More Compassionate Than Male Rats?** All 6 of the 6 female
rats freed the trapped rat ($\hat p_F = 1.0$) while 17 of the 24 male rats
did so ($\hat p_M = 17/24 \approx 0.708$).

- **Best estimate:** $\hat p_F - \hat p_M = 1.0 - 0.708 = 0.292$, estimating
  $p_F - p_M$.
- **Bootstrap SE ≈ 0.093.** As the book's footnote cautions, every bootstrap
  sample contains only the six female values, all yes, so $\hat p_F = 1$ for
  every bootstrap sample — all of the standard error comes from resampling
  the male rats.
- **95% confidence interval:** $0.292 \pm 2(0.093) = 0.105$ to $0.479$ (our
  percentile interval: 0.125 to 0.500).
- Since 0 is not in the interval, it is **not plausible that male and female
  rats are equally compassionate** — the data suggest female rats are more
  likely to show compassion. Still, the interval is wide (few females, a
  proportion pinned at 1), so the size of the difference is uncertain.

*Data:* `data/ch03/CompassionateRats.csv`, from
<https://www.lock5stat.com/datasets3e/CompassionateRats.csv>:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Bootstrap distribution of the difference in proportions of empathy, females minus males
fem = (rats.loc[rats.Sex == "F", "Empathy"] == "yes").to_numpy(float)
male = (rats.loc[rats.Sex == "M", "Empathy"] == "yes").to_numpy(float)
boots = boot_stats([fem, male], lambda r: r[0].mean() - r[1].mean())
boot_plot(boots, "Bootstrap difference in proportions (F - M)")
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
boot_row("Difference (F - M)", fem.mean() - male.mean(), boots).to_string()
```

## Exercise 3.99

**Teens Are More Likely to Send Text Messages.** Teens: $n_t = 800$,
$\hat p_t = 0.87$; adults: $n_a = 2252$, $\hat p_a = 0.72$. Figure 3.23 shows
the bootstrap distribution of $\hat p_t - \hat p_a$ for 5000 bootstrap
samples.

- **(a) SE = 0.015.** The bootstrap differences span roughly 0.10 to 0.20 — a
  range of 0.10, which is about 6–7 standard errors — and the standard error
  must be small enough that $\pm 2\,SE$ stays inside the plot, ruling out
  0.030 and larger. (0.015 also matches the formula
  $\sqrt{\frac{0.87 \cdot 0.13}{800} + \frac{0.72 \cdot 0.28}{2252}}$.)
- **(b)** $0.15 \pm 2(0.015) = 0.12$ to $0.18$: we are 95% sure that the
  proportion of teen cell phone users who send/receive text messages is
  between 0.12 and 0.18 **higher** than the proportion of adults who do so.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Bootstrap distribution of the difference in proportions of texters, teens minus adults
teen = yes_no(round(0.87 * 800), 800 - round(0.87 * 800))
adult = yes_no(round(0.72 * 2252), 2252 - round(0.72 * 2252))
boots = boot_stats([teen, adult], lambda r: r[0].mean() - r[1].mean())
boot_plot(boots, "Bootstrap difference in proportions (teen - adult)")
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
boot_row("Difference (teen - adult)", teen.mean() - adult.mean(), boots).to_string()
```

## Exercise 3.100

**Tea, Coffee, and Your Immune System.** In a randomized experiment, 11
participants drank five or six cups of tea a day and 10 drank coffee; after
two weeks, interferon gamma production was measured (Table 3.12,
`ImmuneTea` data). We estimate the effect size, the increase in average
interferon gamma production for tea compared to coffee.

- **Best estimate:** $\bar x_T - \bar x_C = 34.8 - 17.7 = 17.1$ units.
- **Bootstrap SE ≈ 7.9** (resampling the 11 tea values and the 10 coffee
  values separately, with replacement).
- **95% confidence interval:** $17.1 \pm 2(7.9) = 1.3$ to $32.9$.
- Interpretation: we are 95% sure that the mean interferon gamma production
  for tea drinkers is between about 1 and 33 units **higher** than for
  coffee drinkers. The interval lies (just) above 0, so the data provide
  some evidence that drinking tea enhances interferon gamma production —
  and this was a randomized experiment, so a causal effect is plausible.

*Data:* `data/ch03/ImmuneTea.csv`, from
<https://www.lock5stat.com/datasets3e/ImmuneTea.csv>:

```{python}
#| echo: false
```

## Exercise 3.102

**Correlation between Price and Depreciation in Automobiles.** The
`CarDepreciation` data contain both the **New** price and the
**Depreciation** for the 20 automobile models.

- **(a)** The correlation for the original sample is **$r = 0.126$** — only a
  weak positive association: pricier cars tend to depreciate slightly *more*
  dollars, but the relationship is far from strong.
- **(b)** Bootstrapping the 20 **ordered pairs** (resampling cars, keeping
  each car's New and Depreciation values together) gives **SE ≈ 0.23**.
- **(c)** $0.126 \pm 2(0.23) = -0.33$ to $0.59$: we are 95% sure that the
  correlation between new price and depreciation for all automobile models
  is between about −0.33 and 0.59. Since 0 is in the interval, **zero
  correlation is plausible** — despite $r = 0.126$ in this sample, the data
  do not convince us of a linear relationship. (The percentile interval
  below is shifted further left; with $n = 20$ the bootstrap correlation
  distribution is irregular, another reminder to always look at the plot.)

*Data:* `data/ch03/CarDepreciation.csv`, from
<https://www.lock5stat.com/datasets3e/CarDepreciation.csv>:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Bootstrap distribution of the correlation between new price and depreciation
cars = pd.read_csv("data/ch03/CarDepreciation.csv")
newp = cars["New"].dropna().to_numpy(float)
depv = cars["Depreciation"].dropna().to_numpy(float)
boots = boot_stats([newp, depv], lambda r: np.corrcoef(r[0], r[1])[0, 1])
boot_plot(boots, "Bootstrap correlations")
```

```{python}
boot_row("Sample correlation", np.corrcoef(newp, depv)[0, 1], boots).to_string()
```

## Exercise 3.103

**Headaches and Handedness.** Of 273 participants with cluster headaches,
24 were left-handed; of 477 participants with migraine headaches, 42 were
left-handed.

- **(a)** $\hat p_C = 24/273 \approx 0.088$.
- **(b)** Bootstrapping the 273 cluster cases gives **SE ≈ 0.017** and a 95%
  confidence interval of $0.088 \pm 2(0.017) = 0.054$ to $0.122$: we are 95%
  sure that the proportion of cluster headache sufferers who are
  left-handed is between about 0.05 and 0.12.
- **(c)** $\hat p_M = 42/477 \approx 0.088$.
- **(d)** Bootstrapping the 477 migraine cases gives **SE ≈ 0.013** and an
  interval of about $0.064$ to $0.114$.
- **(e) The migraine interval is narrower.** The two sample proportions are
  identical (0.088), but the migraine sample is larger ($n = 477$ vs
  $n = 273$), so its bootstrap proportions vary less — a larger sample gives
  a smaller standard error and a narrower interval.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Bootstrap distributions of the proportion left-handed, cluster headaches and migraines
cluster_b = boot_stats([yes_no(24, 273 - 24)], lambda r: r[0].mean())
migraine_b = boot_stats([yes_no(42, 477 - 42)], lambda r: r[0].mean())
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7, 3))
for ax, b, name in [(axes[0], cluster_b, "Cluster (n = 273)"),
                    (axes[1], migraine_b, "Migraine (n = 477)")]:
    sns.histplot(x=b, bins=24, ax=ax, color="#4c72b0")
    lo, hi = np.percentile(b, [2.5, 97.5])
    for v in (lo, hi):
        ax.axvline(v, color="#c44e52", ls="--", lw=1)
    ax.set_title(name, fontsize=10)
    ax.set_xlabel("Bootstrap proportions")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
pd.concat([boot_row("Cluster (24 of 273)", 24 / 273, cluster_b),
           boot_row("Migraine (42 of 477)", 42 / 477, migraine_b)],
          axis=1).to_string()
```

person would assign to others in a group.

- **(a)** The parameter is $\mu$, the mean closeness rating that would be
  assigned to other group members (before the activity) by all people like
  these students; the sample mean $\bar x$ estimates it.
- **(b)** $\bar x = 4.87$ on the 1-to-7 scale.
- **(c)** **SE ≈ 0.11** from the bootstrap distribution below.
- **(d)** $4.87 \pm 2(0.11) = 4.65$ to $5.10$.
- **(e)** We are 95% sure that the mean closeness rating assigned to others
  before the activity is between about 4.6 and 5.1 — on average, students
  felt moderately close to their group members even before the activity.

## Exercise 3.105

**Does Synchronization Increase Feelings of Closeness?** We use the
closeness ratings given *after* the activity (**CloseAfter**) to estimate
the difference in mean rating between those who just did a synchronized
activity and those who did a non-synchronized one.

- **(a)** The parameter is $\mu_S - \mu_N$, the difference in mean closeness
  rating between all people who do a synchronized activity and all who do a
  non-synchronized one.
- **(b)** $\bar x_S - \bar x_N = 5.275 - 4.810 = 0.466$ (synchronization is
  associated with closeness about half a scale-point higher).
- **(c)** **SE ≈ 0.23** from the bootstrap distribution below (resampling
  the 138 synchronized and 126 non-synchronized ratings separately).
- **(d)** $0.466 \pm 2(0.228) = 0.009$ to $0.921$.
- **(e)** We are 95% sure that synchronized activity increases the mean
  closeness rating by between about 0.01 and 0.92 points. Since 0 is (just)
  outside the interval, the data provide modest evidence that
  synchronization really does increase feelings of closeness — and this was
  a randomized experiment.

*Data:* `data/ch03/SynchronizedMovement.csv`, from
<https://www.lock5stat.com/datasets3e/SynchronizedMovement.csv>:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Bootstrap distribution of the difference in mean closeness, synchronized minus not
close_y = sync.loc[sync.Synch == "yes", "CloseAfter"].dropna().to_numpy(float)
close_n = sync.loc[sync.Synch == "no", "CloseAfter"].dropna().to_numpy(float)
boots = boot_stats([close_y, close_n], lambda r: r[0].mean() - r[1].mean())
boot_plot(boots, "Bootstrap difference in means (yes - no)")
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
boot_row("Difference (yes - no)", close_y.mean() - close_n.mean(), boots).to_string()
```

  tolerance between all people who complete a synchronized activity and all
  who complete a non-synchronized one.
- **(b)** $\bar x_S - \bar x_N = 224.4 - 211.1 = 13.3$ mmHg.
- **(c)** **SE ≈ 9.2** from the bootstrap distribution below.
- **(d)** $13.3 \pm 2(9.2) = -5.1$ to $31.8$.
- **(e)** We are 95% sure that the difference in mean pain tolerance between
  synchronized and non-synchronized groups is between about −5 and 32 mmHg.
  Since 0 is *within* the interval, a zero effect is plausible — on its own,
  synchronization does not (yet) convince us it boosts pain tolerance.

## Exercise 3.109

**Are Males or Females More Likely to Go to Maximum Pressure?** 33 of the
165 females and 42 of the 99 males allowed the pressure to reach 300 mmHg.

- **(a)** The parameter is $p_F - p_M$, the difference in the proportion who
  would go to maximum pressure between females and males.
- **(b)** $\hat p_F - \hat p_M = 33/165 - 42/99 = 0.200 - 0.424 = -0.224$.
- **(c)** **SE ≈ 0.059** from the bootstrap distribution below (resampling
  the 165 females and 99 males separately).
- **(d)** $-0.224 \pm 2(0.059) = -0.342$ to $-0.106$.
- **(e)** We are 95% sure that the proportion of females who would go to
  maximum pressure is between 0.106 and 0.342 **lower** than the proportion
  of males. Since 0 is not in the interval, the data convince us that males
  are more likely to tolerate the maximum pressure.

*Data:* `data/ch03/SynchronizedMovement.csv`, from
<https://www.lock5stat.com/datasets3e/SynchronizedMovement.csv>:

```{python}
mp = (sync.loc[sync.Sex == "m", "MaxPressure"] == "yes").to_numpy(float)
```

## Exercise 3.110

**NHL Penalty Minutes.** Points and penalty minutes for the 26 Ottawa
Senators players in 2018–2019 (`OttawaSenators2019` data), viewed as a
sample of all NHL players.

- **(a)** The dotplot/histogram of the original penalty minutes (below, left)
  is strongly **skewed to the right**: most players sit between 2 and 35
  minutes while a few outliers stretch up to 56, 75, 81, and 89.
- **(b)** Computed below: **$\bar x = 24.46$ minutes, $s = 24.92$ minutes.**
- **(c)** The bootstrap distribution of the sample mean (below, right) is
  **much more symmetric and bell-shaped than the original data** — averaging
  26 values washes out the skew — and is centered at 24.46.
- **(d)** The standard deviation of the bootstrap means is the standard
  error, **SE ≈ 4.7 minutes** — far smaller than $s = 24.92$, roughly
  $s/\sqrt{n} = 24.92/\sqrt{26}$.
- **(e)** $24.46 \pm 2(4.7) = 15.1$ to $33.9$: we are 95% sure that the mean
  penalty minutes for all NHL players is between about 15 and 34 minutes
  per season.
- **(f)** One team is **not a random sample of the league**: rosters are
  built deliberately (some teams carry an "enforcer" who racks up penalty
  minutes), teams differ in style and discipline, opponents and schedules
  differ, and teammates' minutes are not independent of one another. The
  Senators' mean could be systematically above or below the league mean.

*Data:* `data/ch03/OttawaSenators2019.csv`, from
<https://www.lock5stat.com/datasets3e/OttawaSenators2019.csv>:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Penalty minutes for Ottawa Senators players and the bootstrap distribution of the sample mean
sen = pd.read_csv("data/ch03/OttawaSenators2019.csv")
pen = sen["PenMins"].dropna().to_numpy(float)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7, 3))
sns.histplot(x=pen, bins=12, ax=axes[0], color="#4c72b0")
axes[0].set_title("Original data (n = 26)", fontsize=10)
axes[0].set_xlabel("Penalty minutes")
boots = boot_stats([pen], lambda r: r[0].mean())
sns.histplot(x=boots, bins=24, ax=axes[1], color="#4c72b0")
lo, hi = np.percentile(boots, [2.5, 97.5])
for v in (lo, hi):
    axes[1].axvline(v, color="#c44e52", ls="--", lw=1)
axes[1].set_title("Bootstrap means (5000 samples)", fontsize=10)
axes[1].set_xlabel("Bootstrap sample means")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
boot_row("Sample mean (PenMins)", pen.mean(), boots, digits=2).to_string()
```

## Exercise 3.111

**Standard Deviation of NHL Penalty Minutes.** The sample of 26 Senators
players has a fairly large standard deviation, $s = 24.92$ minutes. We
bootstrap the **standard deviation**: resample 26 penalty minute values with
replacement and compute the standard deviation of each bootstrap sample.

- The bootstrap distribution below is centered near the original $s$ (slightly
  below it, since the sample standard deviation is a biased-high estimate
  corrected only on average) and is noticeably skewed.
- **Bootstrap SE ≈ 4.4.**
- **95% confidence interval (Section 3.3 method):**
  $s \pm 2 \cdot SE = 24.92 \pm 2(4.35) = 16.2$ to $33.6$ minutes: we are
  95% sure that the standard deviation of penalty minutes for all NHL
  players is between about 16 and 34 minutes.
- Because the bootstrap distribution is skewed, the percentile interval from
  our run (14.3 to 31.4) sits a bit lower than the ± 2·SE interval — a good
  example of the two methods disagreeing when the bootstrap distribution is
  not bell-shaped.

*Data:* `data/ch03/OttawaSenators2019.csv`, from
<https://www.lock5stat.com/datasets3e/OttawaSenators2019.csv>:

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: Bootstrap distribution of the standard deviation of penalty minutes
boots = boot_stats([pen], lambda r: r[0].std(ddof=1))
boot_plot(boots, "Bootstrap standard deviations")
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
boot_row("Sample SD (PenMins)", pen.std(ddof=1), boots, digits=2).to_string()
```
